- **The Probe service reports its state, so one machine's service can be seen without asking anyone.** It sends `service.started` once it has found its sessions (its version, and whether the service before it ended without stopping), `service.state` at start, every hour and when something that matters changes (at most every ten minutes), and `service.stopped` with the reason and how long it ran. `service.state` carries counts, yes/no flags, versions, ages and fixed names only: sessions and app windows; recorders (alive, recording, failures, by coding agent) and the tap version; daemon workers by state, their crashes and starts; run holds, imports, hook hosts and queued hook events; background drains and dropped telemetry; the update (on or off, running, its step, whether the last one worked, each step's result, how long since it looked, why it waits); the last answer to each key the CLI holds (sign-in, daemon key, MCP key); the reports the service sent, by kind; and the outbox (pending writes and size, dead letters, held writes, why it is blocked and since when, refused credentials, credential queues, the last error's type, and how many discarded writes it keeps, by the day they were queued). It never sends a session id, run name, path, key or error message. It is sent only when every session whose agent runs allows it (or, with none, the login shell does): `PROBE_TELEMETRY=off` or `PROBE_DIAGNOSTICS=off` there, or a self-hosted server, turns it off. That is asked again whenever the sessions change, and `service.stopped` checks the sessions running at that moment. The outbox part covers every outbox on the machine (a distributed job's `rank-*` ones included) and is left out unless every write it counts (queued, dead-lettered, a multipart upload, discarded) was going to Probe's hosted service. Each file is read once and remembered, so later checks are a listing. It runs on its own timer, so an update that stalls half way is still reported; it looks every few seconds for its first minute, so a service that runs for only seconds is still seen, and sends nothing while it is still finding its sessions. Its reads of the outbox and the config run on threads of their own, so a hung disk never keeps the service from stopping. The answer it reports for each key is the one for the key the config holds now.

## 0.304.1

- **A session whose recorder the Probe service lost is reported once, not every 6 hours.** A session the next service could not resume stays unrecorded until its agent's next prompt registers it again, and an idle agent may not prompt for hours. Its automatic `recorder`/`gone` report was sent again every time the 6-hour dedupe ran out, across service restarts, with nothing new in it: one Codex session sent three in 13.5 hours. The report is now sent once per registration (`watch.json` keeps it); a session that registers again and loses its recorder again is reported again.

- **A full disk stops the Probe daemon with a message saying so, and no longer reports a crash to the Probe team.** When the disk was full, the daemon's session store could not save (SQLite's "database or disk is full"); the daemon stopped, told you only "the daemon crashed (OperationalError: database or disk is full)", and sent a crash report (and, after three in a row, the Probe service sent a crash-loop report). It now says `the daemon stopped: the disk is full (...; its state folder: <folder>); it starts again once there is space` in `probe doctor` and the status line, your agent is told the daemon is "out of disk space" while it records the session itself, and no report is sent. The daemon keeps restarting on the usual crash backoff (30 s, doubling to 30 min). A failed save is rolled back and its events are read again, so nothing is lost. A write that fails with "No space left on device" or a full disk quota counts the same, in the daemon's other error reports too (SQLite reports a full quota as a disk I/O error, which is still reported).

- **A daemon reader turn that a limit told to finish, and that then answered, no longer reports a stopped turn.** The reader's limits (40 model rounds, 300 seconds, its size) tell the model to end its turn, and it then answers as usual; only the size limit's end was quiet, so a turn that reached 40 rounds and answered was reported to the Probe team as "reader turn stopped: 40 model rounds" and marked stopped in the session's status. Now none of them is. A turn cut off before it answered (its time ran out, the model kept calling past the end, or the loop detector stopped it) is still reported.

- **The Probe service no longer reports a laptop that is offline.** Three of its automatic reports to the Probe team fired for a machine with no network: a daemon that handed recording back because its model could not be reached (`worker`/`lease_gateway`), a transcript whose uploads had waited an hour (`capture_stalled`), and three update checks in a row that could not reach the release manifest (`update_failed`). Offline now means no network at all: the server's name did not resolve, or the network or host was unreachable. A refused connection, a timeout, a TLS failure (a proxy that re-signs it) or an answer that is not what was asked for still reports, since it may be ours. The daemon marks such a hand-back `offline` in its lease; a transcript is aged from the last time its uploads were offline, not its last receipt; such an update cycle is kept as `offline: true` and not counted.

- **`probe daemon session search` and `logbook` with no words say how to give them.** They answered the tool's own refusal, "op=logbook needs `query`", and a daemon's next try was `--query`, which is no option either. They now answer `not run: logbook needs the words to look for: probe daemon session logbook "<words>"` with the usage line.

## 0.304.0

- **A session recorded by an older tap's own `tap watch` moves to the Probe service at its next prompt, with no restart.** A session whose capture started while no Probe service could run gets a `tap watch` of its own, and one started by a tap older than 0.10.13 never handed the session to the service once one ran: it stayed on that tap's code for good and got no hints. A new prompt route of the Probe plugin (its hooks always run the installed copy) now finds such a watcher, proves it is this session's (its pid is alive and its command line is this session's `tap watch`), asks the Probe service to record the session with the newest installed tap, and only then stops the old watcher and removes its pid file. The service's recorder continues from the session's saved upload position, so no line is lost or sent twice. Before the old watcher is stopped, the session's Probe daemon is asked to hand over (so it does not end as stopped and tell the agent recording is back with it). The old tap's hooks keep running in that session, so the move also keeps the old tap's prompt hook from starting a new watcher (it dates that tap's ten-minute retry stamp 30 days ahead); a watcher the old tap still starts later (its session start on a `/compact`, which knows no service) is moved the same way at the next prompt, and a moved session that nothing records any more (capture turned off and on, a service gone) is recorded again, at most every 10 minutes. A session whose Probe switch is off is neither moved nor recorded again by it. Each watcher is moved once, in the background, never on the prompt's clock, and the route costs nothing (no Python starts) for a session without such a watcher. If the service will not record the session, the old watcher keeps recording it and the move is tried again after 10 minutes, three times in all; `PROBE_TAP_HOSTED=0` means never. One known cost: a tap older than 0.10.13 sends the session's end signal when it stops, so a moved session is processed once at the move and again at its real end, the same cost a resume onto a newer tap pays. Claude Code and Codex on macOS and Linux (not Windows, where no watcher can be proven this session's).
- **After an update, open sessions get the new status line, the new Probe block in CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md and the new capture code without restarting.** The Probe service now follows its own update: right after it, it refreshes the status line's renderer from the installed plugin copy (the one Claude Code's install ledger names: its user-scope install when it lists a user-scope and a project-scope one, else the newest), runs `probe agent-rules refresh` and `probe notes sync` for the coding agents it records, and restarts itself onto the newest installed tap so the sessions it records run the new capture code. That restart pauses each recording for about a second; it resumes from its saved position, so nothing is lost or sent twice, and the next service starts as soon as the old one has exited. When the update also installed a new CLI, the new service does this once it has started. Before, all three waited for a new session to start, and a swarm left running for 20 minutes after an update still ran the old renderer, block and capture code. A session left open on an older plugin copy can also no longer roll the status line's renderer back to its own older copy at a `/clear` or resume.
- **The first prompt of a session gets its Probe hint within about a second.** The service's hint lane looked at a new session before the session's recorder had taken it, found nothing to read, and then slept until something else woke it, so the first prompt of a session started on its own got its hint about 17 seconds late. The lane now looks again the moment a recorder takes its session.
- **A failed CLI update reads as failed.** An update whose CLI install failed while the plugins updated exited 0 with `complete: false`, and the Probe service recorded it as done: `probe service status` and `probe doctor` said "(ok)", the failure was not counted, and the next try was six hours later. Such an update now counts as failed everywhere (`probe service status`, `probe status`, `probe doctor`, `update.json`), including one an older service recorded, and a failed update is tried again after 1 hour, then 2 and 4, before going back to every 6 hours.
- **The Probe service no longer starts and quits every minute next to sessions it cannot record, and an idle exit or `probe service stop` no longer holds back the next start.** After an update, a session still on a tap from before the service (0.9.x) never asked the service to record it, so the Probe hooks started the service at every prompt or tool call and it quit 20 seconds later, over and over. For 15 minutes after the service exits because nothing needs it, a hook no longer starts it again (and runs its record-keeping work itself instead of queueing it for a service that is not coming), unless another service has started since (one that then crashed leaves no stop record of its own); a session the service records still starts it. A service that stopped on purpose (idle, or `probe service stop`) also no longer counts toward the limit of three starts a minute, which is meant for a service that crashes, so a session starting right after two quick idle exits is no longer left without a service for most of a minute.
- **No more "Restart Claude Code to apply the plugin update" where an update no longer needs one.** `probe update`, the wizard's Update and the update notice told people to restart after every update. Where open sessions follow an update by themselves (Claude Code or Codex on macOS or Linux, a user-scope install, a tap of 0.10.13 or newer, and every session still on an older tap at 0.4.5 or newer, which the new prompt route in the Probe plugin can move), they now say open sessions pick up the new plugin at their next prompt, and the note about sessions still on the old tap says they move to the new one at their next prompt. Everywhere else (Kimi Code, Windows, a project-scope install, a tap older than 0.10.13, a session on a tap before 0.4.5, an old session with only the capture plugin installed) they still say to restart. Turning capture back on or off in the wizard with the capture plugin already installed says it needs no restart; a plugin installed for the first time still says to restart, because sessions already open never loaded it. A Probe daemon handing over to a new daemon process (an update, the service restarting, a resumed session) no longer tells the agent "the daemon is not running, so recording is back with you": it says the daemon is handing over to a new daemon process and there is nothing for the agent to do, and says nothing when it is back. A hand-over no new daemon takes up within 2 minutes (counted from the end of the update's hold on the daemons, for an update that takes longer) is reported like any other stop, and the agent records the work itself again.
- **A `probe` command run during an update runs at once instead of waiting and failing.** While the Probe service updated, every `probe` command, a training loop's `probe log` and every hook's call included, waited up to 10 seconds and then exited 75 ("Probe is updating itself"). An update that installs the new CLI beside the running one (the usual case with a uv install) or updates only the plugins replaces nothing a `probe` command runs from, so commands now run on the installed version right away. Only an in-place update still holds a command back, and even then a hook's call (while the hook's own time limit is still running; a background job a hook left behind waits like any command) or a read-only command (`probe status`, `probe doctor`, `probe --version`, `probe session status`, `probe service status`) answers at once instead of waiting.

## 0.303.1

- **A debug log keeps an agent's part when the agent prunes its sessions mid-scan.** A transcript deleted while `probe doctor --bundle` read the transcripts' dates failed that agent's whole part of the log (`failed: FileNotFoundError`): its transcript list, facts and settings files were left out, and only a working `--version` still named the agent. A deleted transcript is now skipped and the next newest one takes its place in the 10 listed. A session folder deleted during the walk (which fails it on Python 3.10 and 3.11) no longer empties the agent's transcript list: the folder is walked up to 3 times, and a walk that fails every time is named in the log's notes instead of reading as an agent with no sessions. An agent folder this user cannot read (removed meanwhile, or left owned by root after `sudo`) no longer fails the agent's whole part: its version and facts are kept, and the notes say the folder could not be listed. The log's README now heads these lines Notes instead of Trimmed. The same skip, with the next newest taking the place, covers the Probe service's action records in the log, the old debug logs Probe deletes (it keeps the newest 3), and the report copies it keeps: two reports saved at once no longer leave one copy marked as still sending.

## 0.303.0

- **Only the researcher's own answer path can say yes to a question the Probe daemon holds (#3355).** The daemon holds a risky action (a shell command off the safe list, deleting another researcher's data, a team-note change, feedback for the Probe team) until the researcher answers its question, and the Probe service could record that answer for any program of the same user that asked it, including the coding agent's own shell, with whatever source the program named. Each held question now gets a random answer key of its own, kept beside the question in the approvals folder (readable only by you, never shown in a prompt, a refusal or a log), and the service records an answer only from a caller that sends that key: the approvals hook, which reads it when the question tool returns the researcher's pick. Anything else is refused and nothing is written, so the action stays held and the question is asked again. The service now names where an answer came from itself instead of taking the caller's word. The service's `hooks.run`, which runs Probe's hooks for pi, now runs only the events pi's guard sends (a tool check before a shell command, a file write or a Probe tool) and refuses any other, so a made-up event can no longer move a session's Probe switch, record a permission mode or answer a question. The warm hook host (the process that runs Probe's hooks quickly for a plugin folder) now runs an event only for a client that sends the random key it keeps beside its socket in your private temporary folder, so a program that merely reaches the socket can no longer hand it a made-up event; a session on an older plugin is refused there and runs its hooks itself, as it does whenever the host is unavailable. The guard also refuses a shell command that calls the service's mailbox or `hooks.run` itself, that runs one of Probe's own hook programs by hand with an event it wrote, or that touches your hook hosts' folder (`/tmp/probe-<your user number>`; a folder of your own such as `/tmp/probe-42` is not it), and its approvals-folder check now covers the key folder too. It decides by the program a command actually runs and where that file is, following `cd`, nested shells, `eval` and variables to it: a script of your own named `dispatch.py` or `dispatch.sh` runs as before, and reading, listing, copying, committing or testing Probe's hook files, or searching for a mailbox method, is never refused. A missing host key is written again by its host, and a file that is not a key at that path never makes a hook wait. Older pieces stay safe either way: an approvals hook from before this release is refused by the service and writes the answer file itself, as it always could, and a question filed by an older daemon has no key, so its answer is written by the hook the same way. These checks raise the bar to the one the approvals folder already set; a program of the same user that reads that folder or runs Probe's hook code with a made-up event can still answer, as before.

## 0.302.0

- **A session the Probe service records no longer reads "not started" because an old watcher left its pid file behind (tap 0.10.17).** When a session's own watcher gave up or was killed and the Probe service took the session over, the watcher's pid file stayed beside the service's `.hosted` marker. `probe session status`, `probe doctor` and the status line read that pid file first, found its process gone, and said capture was "not started" while the service recorded the session. A pid file whose process is gone (or is some other program now) no longer decides: the service's marker is read next. The session start hook now also removes such a pid file, whether the service takes the session or a new watcher starts, including one whose process id now runs another program, and the prompt hook's quick check no longer reads a pid file that says 0 or 1 (0 meant the hook's own process group, which always exists, so the session was never started again).

- **Ending a session never signals a process that is not its watcher (tap 0.10.17).** The session end hook signalled whatever process the session's pid file named, and its whole process group when that process led one. A pid file left by a watcher that died could name an unrelated program by then, because the system reuses process ids. The hook now signals a process only after its command line shows it is this session's `tap watch`; any other pid file is only removed. The hand-over file one SessionEnd entry leaves for the other (`.stopping`) is never signalled at all: it was read with no check, so a stale one, or one anyone could put in the shared `/tmp`, got its whole process group killed. It is now only waited on, and only while that group still runs this session's `tap watch`; a session start clears it. Watcher files are read only when they are this user's own regular files (never a link, which could point at a terminal and stall the hook).

- **`probe session status` and `probe doctor` say a session is recorded only while the Probe service's recorder actually records it.** A session the service took over read as running for as long as the service process lived, even when its recorder recorded nothing: in a folder listed in `.disabled_paths`, without a pairing token, while the session's own watcher still held it, or while it failed every pass and waited to try again. `probe session status`, `probe doctor` and the status line now ask the service whether its recorder holds the session (one local call, at most 0.5 s; the status line asks once per refresh) and say "not recording" when a live recorder does not hold it (its server does not answer, it waits to try again, or the session's own watcher still holds it), and "not started" when the service records no such session. When the service does not answer, they read the marker as before. The pi self-heal that runs before every `probe` command does not ask: a recorder the service runs is left to it, so it no longer starts a second capture beside one waiting for its server. `probe status --json` gains `service.recorders[].recording`.

- **A session the Probe service has recorded for more than two days keeps reading as recorded (tap 0.10.17).** Every session start deleted every `.hosted` marker older than two days, and nothing rewrites a marker while the service records the session, so a long session read "not started" from its third day on. The cleanup now keeps a marker whose process is this user's running Probe service (on Windows: the process the service's lock file names), and deletes the rest as before.

- **`probe doctor` and `probe status` show a running session whose Probe mode is off as "(off)", not "(ended)".** The service never counts a session in mode off as live, whatever its agent does, so doctor listed every such session as ended while its agent ran, and `probe status` left it out of its count of live sessions. The service now says whether each session's agent still runs (`session.list`'s `agent_live`): doctor shows "(off)" while it does, and `probe status` counts it ("3 live sessions (1 off)"). `probe status --json` gains `service.sessions[].agent_live`.

- **The update report names sessions the Probe service still records on an older tap.** After a tap update, the report said "N sessions started before the update still run tap X" only for sessions with their own watcher process. Sessions the service records run the tap the service loaded, which moves only when a session names a newer one, and the report never mentioned them. It now counts them too, with the tap the service reports for its recorders. A service too old to report it is left out rather than guessed at, and a session that both has its own watcher and is listed by the service is counted once.

- **Windows: `probe session status`, `probe doctor` and the status line find sessions the Probe service records (tap 0.10.17).** The tap's hooks keep their watcher files in Git Bash's `/tmp`, which they pass on as `PROBE_TAP_WATCHER_DIR` only to what they start. The CLI looked in Windows's temp folder instead, and the status line hook did not look on Windows at all. The session start hook now records that folder in the tap's state folder (`.watcher_dir`), and both read it from there. The status line believes a `.hosted` marker only when its pid is the process the service's lock file names, with the same start time, and never probes a process with `os.kill` there (on Windows that sends Ctrl+C to a whole process group). The prompt hook's quick check now also ignores a `.hosted` marker that is not this user's own regular file or names pid 0 or 1: pid 0 meant the hook's own process group, which always exists, and Git Bash trusted any number.

- **`probe session status` and `probe doctor` say "halted" on machines where the tap cannot be imported.** When the server refused the tap's credential (a 401), the tap stopped uploading and recorded that in its state database. The CLI read that record through the tap's own Python modules, which most CLI installs cannot import, so it never said halted there. It now reads the tap's state database directly, read-only and without waiting on a writer, and still compares the refused credential with the current one, so a machine paired again is not reported as halted.

- **pi's `/probe-status` says what `probe session status` says about a session the Probe service records (pi package 0.6.3).** It said "capturing (recorded by the Probe service)" whenever the service's marker named a live service, while pi's footer and `probe doctor` said "not recording" because the service's recorder did not hold the session (its server did not answer, or it was waiting to try again). `/probe-status` now asks the CLI first (`probe session initialize`, which asks the service) and prints its reason, e.g. "not capturing: not recording". `probe session status` and `probe session on` in pi no longer print `"running": false` with the reason "running" for such a session either. pi picks up the new package when it next starts.

- **A pi session that quits and resumes at once keeps being recorded (tap 0.10.17).** pi's quit tells the Probe service's recorder to finish the session. A `pi --continue` within the few seconds that recorder takes to finish read the session as already recorded, so nothing recorded the resumed session once the recorder ended. Now `tap start` treats a session whose end is still being finished as not recorded and asks the service again. The service starts a fresh recorder for it, which takes the session over once the finishing one lets go. The finishing recorder no longer deletes the `.hosted` marker the fresh one wrote, and a recorder now tells the service as soon as it has seen the session's end.

## 0.301.0

- **pi records sessions on a Mac with Apple's Python 3.9, and reads sessions the Probe service records correctly (pi package 0.6.2).** Four fixes to the pi extension. (1) Capture needs Python 3.11 or newer, and pi ran it on the first `python3` on PATH, which on a Mac is Apple's 3.9: the recorder died at once and no pi session was recorded. pi now asks each interpreter its version and uses the first that is new enough, in the order the Claude Code and Codex hooks use since tap 0.10.16: the tap's own `.venv`, `python3`, the Probe CLI's interpreter (the one the Probe service's `runtime.json` names, else uv's tool folder), then `python3.14` down to `python3.11`. When none is new enough, pi says which `python3` it found and leaves that in the tap's state folder, where `probe doctor` shows it. (2) `/probe-status` said "not capturing" for every session the Probe service records, because it looked only for the old per-session watcher's pid file. It now reads the service's `.hosted` marker the way the status line does (the marker must be this user's own file, and name this user's running Probe service: its command line on Linux, its lock file on macOS and Windows) and says "capturing (recorded by the Probe service)". (3) Starting such a session no longer waits 2 seconds and logs "spawn failed?": the service's marker counts as the start being confirmed. (4) Quitting pi and resuming the same session right away could leave the resumed session unrecorded: the quit left the service's marker behind while the service was still finishing the session, and the resume read that as "already recorded". On quit, pi now asks the service to finish the session (`tap finish`, waiting up to 3 seconds for its last upload, as the Claude Code hook does) and removes the marker, so a resume asks the service to record it again. Switching to another session inside pi removes the marker without waiting. pi picks up the new package when it next starts.
- **Writes stuck behind a revoked token are sent again on their own.** A job that ran with its own `PROBE_TOKEN` queues writes that go out only with that token. Once the token was revoked (by a re-login, or by `probe token create`), they waited forever, and signing in again did not help. Now any `probe` command checks for them at most every 10 minutes (every 6 hours after a check that found nothing to send); hooks and the daemon run such commands often. A token counts as dead when the server refused the token itself on one of its writes (a 401, or a 403 saying it was revoked or expired) and no process still running holds it. A refusal for a missing scope never counts. The writes then go out with the login stored on this machine, but only when the server confirms that login is the same team and user, the login is for the same server, and nothing shows the token lacked the scopes those writes need (a job now records its token's scopes). `/ingest` writes, DELETEs and writes Probe refused for scope are never sent this way: those go only with their own credential. `probe doctor` runs the same check at once and reports it (`probe status` only reads). `PROBE_OUTBOX_RESCUE=off` turns the check off, and `probe outbox adopt --credential <fingerprint>` does the same by hand, sending right away, under the same checks. Each rescue reports an `outbox.rescued` event.
- **A job whose `PROBE_TOKEN` is a copy of the stored login keeps working after a re-login.** Its writes are recorded as the login's, so they go out with the new login of the same account. The job re-reads the login after a refusal, and the worker it starts no longer inherits the copy. Before, the job's writes waited until it was restarted, and the ones already queued never went.
- **`probe token create` no longer signs this machine out.** The token was tied to this machine's device, so the server revoked this machine's own login to make room for it. A named token now gets an installation of its own and revokes nothing.
- **`probe outbox status` and `probe outbox drain` name the credential holding writes back and what to do next.** Each one shows its fingerprint, write count, latest refusal and the process holding it (pid, program, release; alive, gone, or unknown for releases that record none). The next step is restarting that process, `probe outbox adopt`, or `probe outbox discard --held --credential`. `adopt` is suggested only when it would pass.

## 0.300.0

- **The status line no longer says a session the Probe service records is not being captured (macOS and Linux).** Claude Code's Probe status line showed "not capturing session transcript: not started" on every tracked session the Probe service records, while `probe session status` said capture was running. Its refresh hook looked only for the old per-session watcher's pid file, and a session the service records has none: the service leaves a `.hosted` marker naming itself instead. The hook now reads that marker, and believes it only when the process it names is this user's Probe service (its command line on Linux, the service's lock file on macOS), so a service that stopped without handing its sessions on never reads as recording. It now also says "halted" when the tap stopped uploading after the server refused its credential (a 401), where it used to say capture was running or not started. It reads only watcher files that are this user's own regular files, so another user's file in the shared `/tmp` can neither change the answer nor stall the status line. Sessions already open need no restart: their hooks run from the newest installed plugin, so the status line corrects itself at the next refresh after the update. Windows still shows "not started" for these sessions; that is a separate fix.
- **The Probe service reports a stuck outbox, a refused key and stalled session capture.** Three new watch families, each reported the way the service's other failures are (`POST /v1/diagnostics/reports`, with the same consent and 6 h dedupe), every one a machine report: `outbox_stuck` when one outbox queue (the root, a credential queue or a delivery namespace, judged on its own) holds writes nothing on the machine will send without a person (a credential the API refused, or writes held for one; a run close waiting on its data is not), that queue's oldest write an hour old, on two checks five minutes apart (counts only, never a fingerprint); `capture_stalled` when live sessions' transcripts have waited an hour past their last receipt (or, for a session none of whose batches ever landed, an hour with its receipt cursor not moving), one report naming up to 8 of them, so a server-side ingestion stall is one report per machine; `credential_refused` when the API refuses a key the CLI config holds: the login and the MCP key asked `GET /v1/me`, the daemon key `POST /v1/device-state` (which records no use of it), once a day per key, only with the consent its report would need, only over HTTPS, never redirected, and reported once per key. The checks run every 5 min from the first scan (a report 5 min into a session, not 10); the key check runs beside the scan and the outbox read on its own thread, each given up past its deadline, so a slow server or a hung mount holds neither the scan nor the service's exit. An outbox or capture report waiting for a retry is dropped once a check no longer sees its condition. A customer's 9,061+ writes sat behind a revoked credential for 26 h on 2026-10-22; until now only the CLI banner said so, and only when someone ran `probe`.
- **A failed automatic report is tried again instead of silencing its family for 6 hours.** The watch settled an incident before its report child ran and retried only once-ever reports, so a diagnostics 503 or a timeout held a recurring family back for the whole dedupe window with nothing sent. Every report is now tried again every 30 min for a day (2 h after a rate limit) until it is taken (`sent`, `deduped` or `disabled:*`); one refused for its credentials or too large is not, because the child keeps its claim of the window and a retry would only answer `deduped`.
- **A machine whose every key is refused still reaches us.** When an automatic report is refused (401/403) with the CLI token and the daemon key alike, the report child sends one `service.report_undeliverable` telemetry event (family and reason, both slugs), at most once per family per machine per 6 h; the PostHog destination "Report undeliverable" posts it to #eng-alerts. A signed-out machine, holding no key, sends nothing.
- **`outbox.stuck` reports held writes.** The outbox status now folds `held` from the credential queues and the delivery namespaces, which it did not (a held queue under an empty root said nothing), records each queue's run-close holds apart (`close_held`), and names the queue blocked longest (`blocked_oldest_pending`, `blocked_reason`). `outbox.stuck` fires, without a banner, once one queue has held writes for a credential nothing here holds for an hour, and carries `held` and `refused_credentials` counts.

## 0.299.3

- **A Codex session keeps being recorded across the Probe service's self-update.** When the service restarts, it resumes every session it was recording. It loaded the tap from each session's saved plugin folder in turn, and a session whose folder was gone was dropped without a word. Its entry was then erased from `recorders.json`, so nothing recorded it until its agent's next prompt. Codex removes a plugin's old version folder when it installs a new one, and an update cycle does exactly that just before it restarts the service. So the first Codex session in line stopped being recorded at every update that bumped the tap: on one Mac (2026-10-24, CLI 0.299.0, tap 0.10.15 → 0.10.16) the new service resumed 7 sessions but not the open Codex one, and its watch reported the Codex session's recorder `gone` 107 s later. Now the service picks one tap first and resumes every session on it, so one session's missing folder no longer decides anything. A folder that is gone moves to the highest-numbered version folder beside it that holds a tap, along with the session's saved `PLUGIN_ROOT`. A session that still cannot resume is named in `service.log` with the reason, and its agent's next prompt asks the service again; one resumed on an older tap than its own (its own would not load) is named there too.

## 0.299.2

- **A debug log names only the coding agents on the machine.** Since 0.298.1 every log was filed under all 4 coding agents Probe knows (Claude Code, Codex, pi, Kimi Code), because each one's folder in the log always holds two records, even for an agent that is not installed, so staff filtering logs by agent matched every log. An agent now counts when the log holds its version (its own program on PATH answered `--version`; another package's `pi` is not pi, as in the wizard), a recent transcript, or a file from its settings folder.

## 0.299.1

- **One stuck update no longer stops a machine's automatic updates for good.** The Probe service waited for its update with no time limit. An update that never finished kept the service's update in progress, so every later check answered "running" and nothing updated again. A service started after that one found the stuck update's setup lock and waited on it forever, because a setup lock is never taken over. Now an update runs 30 minutes at most (normal ones take under a minute). Past that the service stops it: SIGTERM first, so the update can let go of its locks and say how it ended, then SIGKILL 30 seconds later. The update fails, and the next one can run. A service that finds a stuck update left by the service before it stops that one the same way first, and only when it can prove which process it is: the update record names it, it is still that same process (not a reused process id), and it is running Probe's update. A person's `probe wizard` and the app's Update action are never stopped. `probe doctor` shows the stopped update as failed ("the update ran past 30 min and was stopped"), and the update report to the server says it was stopped instead of sending only the parts that finished.

## 0.299.0

- **Session capture runs on a Mac whose `python3` is Apple's 3.9 (tap 0.10.16).** The tap needs Python 3.11 or newer, and its hooks ran it on the first `python3` on PATH. On a stock Mac every `python3 -m tap` (owner, record, watch, finish) died on `ImportError: cannot import name 'StrEnum'`, which the hooks swallowed: no session was recorded and no daemon started, while the Probe plugin's own hooks (fine on 3.9) kept working and `probe doctor` said "capturing". The hooks now run the tap on the first interpreter that is new enough: the plugin's own `.venv`, `python3`, the Probe CLI's interpreter (the one the service's `runtime.json` names, else `~/.local/share/uv/tools/probe-research/bin/python`), then `python3.14`..`python3.11` (on Git Bash, the CLI's `%LOCALAPPDATA%` and `%APPDATA%` paths); they still parse their payloads with plain `python3`. SessionStart remembers its choice in `.python` in the tap's state folder, so SessionEnd's `tap finish` runs there too without starting a python inside Claude Code's 1.5 s exit budget. With none, the session start says so to the researcher once a session ("Probe is not recording this session: ...") and leaves what it found in `.python-missing` in the tap's state folder, and `probe doctor` shows the capture Status as "not running: needs Python 3.11 or newer (python3 3.9.6)" with a warning, instead of "capturing".

- **A `probe` command run outside a terminal now asks the Probe service to update, and no longer records that it skipped.** Where the Probe service is the machine's updater (macOS and Linux), a command that finds a newer CLI used to apply the old updater's rules first: no update from a command outside a terminal, from a training-run command, or while a run was live. Each such command saved a skip, "not an interactive terminal", although it could only ever have asked the service. A coding agent's hooks and the Probe daemon run `probe` outside a terminal all the time, the session-start hook's own `probe service check-now` included, so one laptop saved 293 of these skips in three hours (2026-10-23). Each skip replaced the service's own reason for waiting (a setup running, a daemon recording) in the record that `probe doctor` prints and the server's update report sends. A machine that started no new session also waited up to six hours for the service's next scheduled check. Now such a command asks the service at most once every 15 minutes, from a terminal or not and with a run live or not, and saves nothing; the service decides and records its own reason when it waits. `probe service ...` itself, the training-run commands (`log`, `span`, `artifact`, `run`, `exec`, `outbox`) and the commands the service runs itself (its team-note sync) still start nothing, and commands that start together ask once. Windows, and an install with no service, keep the old rules.

## 0.298.1

- **A debug log is filed under every session and coding agent it holds.** The server listed only the sessions live at the moment it was sent (one, in the first live check, for a log holding 11 session folders, and no coding agent), so staff searching by a session or an agent missed it. It now names each session it has a folder for and each coding agent whose settings it collected.

## 0.298.0

- **The Probe service tells the Probe team when something in it breaks (tap 0.10.15).** It now notices its own failures and sends one automatic diagnostic report for each (through `probe.core.run report`), instead of leaving them as lines in `service.log`: a recorder that fails 3 times in 15 minutes while its agent runs, or that stopped making progress for 5 minutes (or whose own `tap watch` went silent for 90 seconds), a daemon worker that gives up or crashes 3 times in a row, a service that died without stopping (found by the next one: SIGKILL or OOM, never a reboot, a stop on purpose or a Windows logoff), 3 unhandled exceptions in 15 minutes (now logged with their traceback, at most 3 times per kind in 15 minutes, and a fatal signal's too), a release the guard switched back from (once per version), 3 failed update cycles in a row, a tap that would not load (once per version, tried again for a day until the report goes through: an automatic report that failed offline, on the server or its rate limit now gives its 6-hour window back), 3 hook events in 15 minutes that timed out or lost their host, and background work that failed at its start. The OS keeper now counts a service as up only when it answers, and reports one that a session needed and that did not answer for 5 minutes of the machine being awake. Whether a report may be sent is decided when the failure happens: a report about a session needs that session's consent; a report about the machine needs that of every session whose agent runs then (Probe off included) and of the environment it happened in, and a no is never sent later. `PROBE_TELEMETRY=off`, `PROBE_DIAGNOSTICS=off` or a self-hosted `PROBE_BASE_URL` turns them off, and a hook that exits 2 (a Stop message, a veto) is never a failure. Nothing is reported while an update hands the workers over, and nothing measured in time counts in the 5 minutes after the machine wakes from sleep. At most one report runs at a time, it is stopped after 60 seconds, and each (kind, session) is asked about at most once every 6 hours; `probe status`'s service record shows the last five and what they answered. The tap's registration now says whether its session allows reports, its hosted recorder marks its progress for the service, and when the tap gives up on a session's daemon worker it marks the worker's lease `error` instead of letting it lapse.

- **`probe doctor --send` sends the Probe team a diagnostic report of this machine and prints its id.** The report holds versions, how Probe is installed, the Probe service's records (its guard, how it last stopped, its recent starts, its updater) and the tails of its logs, `daemon-errors.log` and, for a session, its daemon worker's and recorder's logs. Credentials, this machine's home folder and login name, conversations, daemon stores and approvals are left out, and so is any session not recorded under this account's server and daemon key. The newest 5 reports stay in `~/.local/state/probe/daemon/reports/`, so a report that could not be sent (offline, rate limited) is still on the machine. The agent rules name it (managed block v48), and `probe doctor` shows a "Diagnostic reports" row: on (and the last one sent), or off and why. The Probe service will send the same report on its own when a daemon worker, a recorder or the service misbehaves (next release), never when `PROBE_TELEMETRY` or `PROBE_DIAGNOSTICS` is off or the server is not Probe's hosted service, and at most once per incident every 6 hours; it asks for one with `python -I -m probe.core.run report`.

- **`probe doctor --bundle` saves a debug log, and `--send` sends it to the Probe team.** One zip with `probe doctor` and `probe status`, the Probe service's folder and its live answers, every live session's and the 10 most recent sessions' worker and recorder logs, each coding agent's version, settings and Probe plugins, recent transcripts by size, line count and model (never their content), this system's state, the environments of this command, the service and each agent process, and a reachability check. Every value under a credential-like name, header values, OAuth and account blocks and prompt history are left out; a config that does not parse is listed, never copied; command lines keep only the program and flag names, and only this user's processes are listed; home folder paths stay. Each log is its last 5 MiB and the zip at most 25 MiB (oldest log lines go first, and its README says so); a source that fails or stalls for 10 s keeps the files it finished and is listed. A daemon audit report that has no mailbox to go to is no longer written whole to the worker's log. The newest 3 stay in `~/.local/state/probe/debug/` (`--out` picks another folder), and `--json` prints one JSON object last, for the desktop app.

- **`daemon-errors.log` moves to `daemon-errors.log.1` past 1 MiB, and every line is scrubbed of credentials and this machine's home folder before it is written.**

## 0.297.0

- **The daemon now tells a message from another agent apart, and makes room for Probe hints next to the reader's messages.** A message another agent sends a session (another Claude Code session's cross-session message, a helper agent's SendMessage, a Codex helper's final answer) used to reach the daemon as an anonymous harness line, or, from a Codex helper, not at all. It is now marked as a peer agent's message, with who sent it and the message without its wrapper, and the daemon's reader and writer see it as one (`[peer agent · <sender> · <id>]`). The ML gate reads these messages too (`[peer agent]` lines in what it sends Probe) and treats a new one like a new prompt (one that reaches a busy agent between its steps, such as a helper's report, belongs to the turn under way), so a session another agent drives is no longer judged on its tool calls alone; while the gate holds a session (or would, in shadow), another agent's messages ask again at most every 5 minutes, since agents write far faster than people. The mailbox gives a hint from the Probe service (`origin: "hint"`) a slot of its own: one hint and one reader message can both reach the agent in the same turn, a newer hint replaces only an older waiting hint (an older one that arrives late is dropped, for the reader's messages too), nothing of the reader's removes a hint, and a hint shows as it came only when it is a message Probe framed (`[Probe] ...`). The claim log now records each delivered message's origin. The Claude Code and Codex hook and pi's extension follow the same rules. Probe can also switch off, per team, the reader's turn at each researcher prompt (`x-probe-reader-prompt-wake: off`, or `PROBE_READER_PROMPT_WAKE=off` on the machine); it stays on unless Probe says otherwise, and asks and the reader's regular check-ins are unchanged.

- **A session that started while the Probe service was restarting moves to it seconds after its first line, not a minute later (tap 0.10.14).** Such a session gets its own `tap watch`, which offers the session to the service once the transcript has proven whose it is (tap 0.10.13). A session just started has no transcript yet (Claude Code writes it with the first prompt), so the watcher's first look proved nothing, and its next look, and with it the first offer, came a whole minute later: in one Windows live run the service had been back, with the same tap, for 57 s and 68 s when the two late sessions first offered theirs, and they were recorded by the service in 2 of 11 and 3 of 8 checks (every line still uploaded once). Now, for the first 3 minutes of a `tap watch`, the watcher silently rechecks its transcript every 5 s until it can prove whose it is, and then makes its pass and its offer at once (those reads log nothing; passes keep their own cadence), and an offer that no service answers (none runs yet, or it is too busy to answer before the ask's 2 s connect and call timeouts) is made again 5 s later, at most 37 times in those 3 minutes. After that, and for an ordinary refusal (the service answered and said no), the minute stands; a service restarting onto a newer tap, one too old to confirm a hand-over and a refusal for a sandbox keep their own intervals (10 s, 10 minutes, never). Nothing is offered or uploaded before the transcript proves whose it is, as before. The watcher's log now says, once each time it changes, why the session stays with it (no service answered, the service restarts, or the reason it refused).

- **The Probe service can show a coding agent the team's records nearest to what it is doing (Probe hints).** When a session the service records gets a researcher prompt, a message from another agent session, a web search or fetch, or a Probe run launch (`probe exec` opening a new run, or `probe run start`), the service asks Probe (`POST /v1/hints`) for the team's nearest records, leaving out the session's own and, for another session's message, the sender's (found from its socket in Claude Code's session records). Nothing waits on it: the service reads the session's transcript on its own thread, one request goes out at most every 10 s per session and about 20 a minute per machine (a 429 holds that key for a minute; a team whose setting is `off` is asked at most once per 10 minutes per key), the same text is never asked twice, credentials in it are replaced before it leaves the machine (the scan everything Probe records goes through), and any error simply means no hint. When the team's setting answers `on` and the records are close enough, the hint is put in the session's Probe mailbox and the agent sees it at its next prompt or tool call, in daemon and inline sessions alike. A hint whose records the session was already shown is not sent again (a record that changed counts as new), each request names the records already shown so Probe can leave them out, and a hint still waiting when the agent's turn ends or a newer prompt arrives is taken back. Daemon sessions also send the daemon's ML-work verdict for the session. The team's setting is off by default, so nothing is shown until it is turned on (`shadow` only logs what would have been shown); `PROBE_HINTS=off` in a session's environment turns hints off for it, and folders `.probe.config` turns off are never looked up, nor is a command you run yourself with `!` (its output is never sent) or a session whose Probe address or key comes from its environment. The service logs one line per lookup (never the text).

## 0.296.1

- **A failed update report now says what failed.** Some machines told the server an update had failed while the CLI, the plugin and the tap each read "updated" or "current", with no reason given (four machines on 10-22 and 10-23, updating from CLI 0.285.0, 0.292.0 and 0.295.0). The failure belonged to something the report did not show: pi's package failing on a Claude Code or Codex pass, a coding agent with no Probe plugin in it whose update command failed because there was nothing to update, or a plugin list that could not be read. When the Probe service's update ran one pass per agent, a failed pass's result also lost to a pass that had not failed. Now a failed update always names the failing step in the report: pi's failure fills the plugin slot (marked pi), an unreadable Codex or Kimi Code plugin list is an error with its message, a tap still behind says by how far, and a failed pass's failure wins in the merged report. Two rules now agree. A coding agent that has none of Probe's plugins, before or after the update, is not a failed update, and no longer prints the commands to update them by hand; it reads "not installed", as an agent missing from PATH does. A tap the update removed (installed before, gone after) is a failed update; before, it read "not installed (skipped)" with the update marked OK.

## 0.296.0

- **A recorder never sends a session it recovers unless that session's own transcript is in its file (tap 0.10.13).** Every recorder also finishes other sessions on the machine whose recorder went away. It checked that a session's file still began with what had already been sent, but for a session nothing had been sent of yet that check proves nothing: if the file had since come to hold another session's transcript, the recorder uploaded it under the first session's id and could mark it finished (this predates this release). Now each recovered session's file must name that session before anything of it is set aside, staged or sent; a file that names another session sends nothing and is retried later.
- **The service's recorder of a just-started session says it records it from the start (tap 0.10.13).** A session's transcript has no line yet when its recorder starts, and the recorder used to take the session only once a line proved whose transcript it was, at its next pass a minute later: for that minute the service listed the session's recorder as alive but not recording (6 of 13 checks in one live run), although every line still arrived. The recorder now takes the session on its first pass, from the server's answer alone, and checks the transcript once it has a line; when the server cannot be reached it waits as before. Nothing is sent before that check passes, and a transcript that turns out to be another session's makes the recorder let go of the session at once, so the right recorder can take it. The same holds for `tap watch`.
- **A session that started while the Probe service was out of reach moves to the service once it is back (tap 0.10.13).** When the service could not take a session at its start (it was restarting after an update, or the start ran past its 10 s limit on a slow Windows machine), the session got its own `tap watch` and kept it for its whole life: in one live run, two sessions started the moment an update landed were recorded by the service in none of 11 and none of 7 checks (every line still uploaded). Now that `tap watch` asks the service about once a minute whether it will record the session. When the service says yes, the watcher finishes the batch it is on, lets go of the session, and waits for the service's recorder to take it; it leaves only once the service says its recorder holds the session, and its wrapper stops with it instead of starting another. The service carries on from where the watcher stopped, so no line is lost or sent twice, and the session's daemon worker, if any, is handed over too. If the service has not taken the session within a minute, the watcher takes it back, keeps recording, tells the service's recorder to stand down, registers the session again only once the service confirms that recorder is gone (an unanswered check never counts; capture goes on meanwhile, and a session that ends meanwhile gets its last pass at once), and asks again ten minutes later. A session that ends during the hand-over lets its daemon worker finish its queue. A service that refuses because the session runs in a sandbox is never asked again. Works on Linux, macOS and Windows, and needs no new service method: a service from before CLI 0.294.0, which cannot say whether its recorder holds a session, is not offered one.

## 0.295.0

- **The Probe service no longer opens a hidden copy of the desktop app to update it (tap 0.10.12).** Its update cycle used to run `open -g Probe.app --args --background-update` whenever the app was closed and its last check was 6 hours old; while the app was open it recorded no check, so the first cycle after you closed the app started a hidden Probe for a few seconds (a Dock icon, "Stop Running in Background") only to repeat the check the app had made at its launch. Now the service only decides when the app checks and records what happened; the app's own signed updater still does the checking and installing. When the app is open, the cycle sends one `app.check` event, to the newest app connection that takes it, and the step reads `delegated` (that connection closing before a report fails the check, due again); when it is closed the step is `skipped: app_closed`, nothing is launched, and the check waits for the app's next launch. At its launch the app can ask `update.check_now {trigger: "app", app: {version}}` and the answer carries `app: {due, reason}`; the app reports what its updater did with the new method `update.app_result {result: updated|current|failed, version_before, version_after, error}`, which becomes the cycle's `app` step (same state file, same `update.step` events). A report names its check by `cycle_id`: one for an earlier check, or a second report of the same check, changes nothing. A check that never reports within 12 minutes reads as failed and is due again; a failed one is due again at the next launch, and `force` (a person's "Check for updates") never starts a second check while one is under way. A check the older service recorded counts only when it found the app current or updated it. The app can also report `ready` (a newer app is downloaded and verified and installs when it quits): the check then never times out, no second check is sent while that update waits, and the check closes with one final `updated` or `failed`, or, if the app quit without saying, at its next launch, by the version it runs (the downloaded one: updated; any other: due again). `update.status` gains `app` (`due`, `reason`, `last_check`, `listening`, `last`), and `service.hello` lists `update.app` in `caps`. An older app gets none of this unless it asks, and keeps checking at its own launch; a caller in a sandbox cannot record a result (API v1, additive).

## 0.294.0

- **Each release is now checked against the ones already out, and both ways the tap records a session.** The tap's recorder is tested end to end under both of its hosts, `tap watch` and the Probe service, with the same checks: every transcript line reaches the server once and in order, the session is finalized at its end or when its agent is killed, a crashed host resumes without losing or repeating a line, an outage loses nothing, a folder switched off sends nothing more, and a credential in the transcript never leaves the machine. A new CI check installs from PyPI the previous CLI release, the oldest one still supported and the oldest supported one that has the Probe service, and confirms each works with the current service and that the current CLI and tap work with its own service (a release from before the service only has to install and run). The 5 h live run that gates each Probe service release can now be started from main by hand (`gh workflow run live-run.yml`), and it always ends with a report: a command it runs can no longer hold it, and an end phase that overruns writes what the run has. Nothing changes for an install.
- **The Probe service says which sessions it records right now.** The service's status (`service.status` `recorders`) now gives each session it records a `recording` field: true only while its recorder holds the session (it records every line), false while it waits to try again because something else holds it (the session's own `tap watch`). Before, a waiting recorder read as recording. Nothing else changes.

## 0.293.1

- **On macOS, a pi tool call whose hooks run past their wait now warms the plugin folder for the next one.** The Probe service starts a warm hook process for a plugin folder after an event runs without one, but when the event ran past its wait (`hooks.run`'s 300 ms by default), stopping it on a Mac takes longer than the service waits for its answer (macOS has no `os.waitid`), and the service answered "timed out" without starting the warm process. A slow first call could then leave every later call starting its hooks cold, past the wait, with pi's built-in guard deciding alone. The service now starts the warm process when that late answer arrives.

## 0.293.0

- **The tap stops re-sending a session the server holds differently (tap 0.10.9).** When two taps on one machine both captured a session, the server kept one copy and the other tap's next batch was refused for good (409 "batch identity already accepted with different content" or "session owned by another stream"), so it sent that batch again every few seconds for days: one team's 7 sessions, 10-19 to 10-23. Now, once the server's accepted bytes are proven to be the transcript's own first bytes, the tap drops the refused batch and continues the server's stream from where it ends, so nothing is lost or sent twice; an ended session is continued the same way the next time its tap looks at it. A stream over different bytes is never continued, and a session refused again within 10 minutes of being continued waits out its conflict instead, so two taps cannot trade refusals forever.
- **A training run hands its background work to the Probe service when one runs (tap 0.10.10).** The SDK used to fork its own detached processes beside a training loop: the outbox's drainer and, with `PROBE_BOX=1`, the box watcher; and it sent client telemetry itself, so an exiting process could wait up to 3.5 s on PostHog. When a Probe service runs on the machine, the SDK now asks it instead, in one call that waits a quarter second at most, finding the service included (all of it on a thread of its own, so a stalled home folder cannot hold the run): the service starts the same drainer or watcher on the run's own interpreter, in its folder, as its child (one per outbox or box registry, at most 8 drains at once; a child that never starts properly is stopped), and sends the telemetry batch from its own thread (each batch carries an id and each event a uuid, so a batch resent after a lost answer counts once; a stopping service still sends what it took, for up to 3.5 s). The outbox files stay the only record: a drainer keeps delivering if the service stops or updates under it, and the outbox's own lock still keeps one drainer per outbox across every process. Credentials never cross: a process with a Probe credential in its environment (`PROBE_TOKEN` and the like) keeps forking its own drainer, and the service's children deliver with the stored login. With no service, an older one, Windows, a run inside a sandbox, or a proxy or certificate setting for telemetry, everything works as before. New Probe service methods `outbox.drain`, `box.watch` and `telemetry.send` (API v1, additive). Also: the service now runs no work for a caller it cannot rule out being sandboxed, by one rule for every method that runs or stores work (an action, an update check, a status refresh, registering, recording or finishing a session, the hooks, holds, manifest refreshes and these hand-offs); reads, and ending what is the caller's own, still answer. On Linux that includes any caller running with `no_new_privs`, which may hold a Landlock sandbox the service cannot see: its warm hook host, hosted recording and these hand-offs then fall back to the per-session paths (hooks run in place, `tap watch` records, the SDK forks), which on a machine where every process has it (a container with `no-new-privileges`, a Kubernetes pod with `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false`) means everywhere, and a process with it no longer starts a service it could not use. Running the agent as root with CAP_SYS_ADMIN is outside what this protects: such a process can hold a Landlock sandbox without `no_new_privs`, and the service cannot tell. `probe capture off` from inside a sandbox no longer reads the service's refusal as "run this again": it reads what the service records and either succeeds (nothing of that agent) or names the recordings still running, which stop on their own within seconds, and how to stop them now. pi's tool guard, refused by the service, runs the same Python pre-tool hooks itself (pi package 0.6.1) instead of only its built-in port.
- **The status line, the team note's sync, approved imports and `probe wizard --action ... --yes` now go through the Probe service (tap 0.10.11).** The status line's background read is made by the service for every session on the machine at once, at most every few seconds, instead of by a new process per session after tool calls. The team note's sync (at a session's start, after every turn and at its end) runs once per machine, a burst of sessions' syncs as one run, instead of a `probe` per session per event. An approved import's worker is started and watched by the service: it no longer depends on the terminal that started it, a worker that fails to start is still reported as failed, and `probe status` and `probe doctor` list it while it runs. `probe wizard --action configure|recorder|logout|uninstall|update --yes` makes its change through the service as the desktop app does, its output shown in the terminal as before and Ctrl-C still cancelling a browser approval. With no service running, an older one, a `probe` that is not the installed CLI, or a token set in the environment, each works exactly as before; the interactive wizard, `--json` runs, sign-in flags and a configure without `--agent` are unchanged. The service's `action.run` now refuses any caller in a sandbox (an agent's sandboxed shell), whatever client it says it is; released services did not check, so `probe wizard` sends its action only to a service that says it does (`caps: ["action.sandbox"]` in `service.hello`) and otherwise runs it in-process, inside the sandbox. New Probe service methods `statusline.refresh`, `notes.sync` and `import.start` (API v1, additive; tap 0.10.4 carries their client calls).

## 0.292.0

- **The Probe service now owns the daemon's messages to your agent, and an idle Claude Code session wakes for them at once (tap 0.10.7).** The daemon posts its answers, run alerts and held questions through the service, and the hooks take each message, and record your answer to a held question, through it; the service writes the same files the daemon and hooks wrote themselves, and wakes the waiting session the moment a message lands. An idle session no longer runs a Python process that looks at its files every 2 s (every 0.5 s while an ask is open) for up to 7 days: it sleeps until the service says something changed. The service also looks at the waiting sessions' files once for the machine (every 0.25 s for 3 minutes after anything changes, else every 2 s), for a daemon or hook that writes them directly, and asks Probe for every daemon session's run alerts once a round on one kept connection instead of each daemon asking on its own. Measured with 20 waiting sessions on Linux: an answer or a run alert wakes the agent in 15 ms (median; was 0.32 s for an answer and 1.6 s for a run alert), 20 sessions waiting with asks open cost 0.28 s of CPU a minute, service included (was 0.61 s), 20 idle ones 0.08 s every 2 minutes (was 0.31 s), and one idle session no more than before. The files stay the record, so with no service running, an older one, one that stalls or stops mid-delivery, a daemon or hook from before this release, or pi's own reader, everything still works on the files directly and no message is lost or shown twice. A daemon whose key or Probe address comes from its environment keeps asking for its run alerts itself, a caller inside a sandbox writes and takes its own messages, and a session registered from inside a sandbox is never polled for. The service's API v1 gains `mailbox.post`, `mailbox.claim` and `mailbox.answer`, the `mailbox.changed` and `approvals.changed` events for named sessions (`events.subscribe` takes `sessions` and `state_dir`), and a `watched` count in `service.status`.
- **The desktop app's "Last received" and "Pending" are true again, and the app can ask the Probe service for them directly (tap 0.10.8).** Both columns came from the recorder's old upload queue (`state.db`), which stopped moving when capture moved to the transcript journal on 2026-09-08: on one machine Claude Code read "Last received 12 Sep, 104 pending" while it was uploading every few seconds. They now come from each live session's journal: when the server last took its transcript (stamped by the recorder from tap 0.10.6 on, so blank until a session's next upload) and the complete lines it has not taken yet, counted only for the account you are signed in to (after switching accounts, the old account's uploads no longer hide the new one's failures). `session.list` (and `probe status --json`, under `service.sessions` and a new `service.harnesses`) carries the same per session and per agent, each naming the account it belongs to. New Probe service method `desktop.request` (API v1, additive) answers the app's management requests (backfills, jobs, delivery, profile, onboarding) with exactly what `probe desktop request --json` prints, from a child running the same code, so the app no longer needs to start the CLI for them; it refuses exactly what the CLI refuses inside a coding agent's session the Probe daemon records, for the session the asking process runs in; `python -m probe.service.client socket` now also prints the legacy socket, the service and runtime paths and the machine key. Contract: `agent/docs/desktop-service-management.md`. With a service from before this release the CLI reads the journals itself; with no service the app runs the CLI as before, and the columns stay blank (they cover live sessions only).

## 0.291.0

- **The tap's SessionEnd wait fits Claude Code's and Codex's budgets on macOS (tap 0.10.4).** The wait counted 0.2 s sleeps, and on a Mac each one takes about 0.24 s, so it ran past the 1.5 s Claude Code gives SessionEnd at exit (1.6 s: "Hook cancelled") and past Codex's 3 s (3.3 s). It now ends at a deadline measured from the hook's start: 1.1 s under Claude Code's default, 2.6 s under Codex, at most 15 s, on macOS and Linux alike, and still as soon as the session's last upload is done. A Codex session still running two SessionEnd entries from an older plugin now waits for that upload in either order (it did not when the other entry ran first), and when the Probe service records the session, a service that does not answer no longer keeps the hook past the budget.
- **The Probe service now runs the Probe daemon's worker itself for the sessions it records, and no session gets a second worker waiting forever (tap 0.10.5).** For a session the service records, it starts the session's daemon worker from the CLI's own Python and restarts it by the same rules `tap watch` uses: at once after a clean exit, after a doubling wait (30 s, up to 30 minutes) after a crash, not again after "no key" until the session's switch moves, at most five starts a minute. It stops the worker when the session ends, starts none while an update is moving the CLI (the next one starts once the update is done), and `service.status` lists each worker with its state (new field `workers`, API v1, additive). Neither the service nor `tap watch` now starts a worker while another live worker of the same session holds its lock: it asks that worker to hand over and starts the next one once it lets go. A worker that still finds the lock held gives up after 5 minutes and is started again later, where before it waited forever; a test machine had piled up about 100 such waiting workers when its supervisor lost track of one. Sessions recorded by `tap watch`, an older service or an older tap work as before.
- **On Windows, every Probe plugin hook runs.** An event with more than one hook (most tool events) started each through `/bin/bash`, which is no program Windows can start, so those hooks never ran there and said nothing; they now run under the Git Bash the agent's hooks use.
- **On Windows, a command that finds a CLI update no longer stalls for 10 s, and the update no longer waits 30 min to start.** The update ran in the command's own console and waited for the command to exit, and Windows never answered that the command had exited, so the command waited its 10 s on the update and the update its full 30 min on the command. It now runs in its own process group with no window (out of your terminal's Ctrl-C) and starts once the command exits.
- **The Probe service runs on Windows (tap 0.10.6).** It listens on a named pipe only your Windows user can open (and checks the process answering on it runs as you), keeps its files in `%LOCALAPPDATA%\probe\service`, and records your agent sessions itself there, so capture no longer depends on Git Bash running a background recorder. A Task Scheduler task (on battery too) starts it again if it stops while recording. The CLI still updates itself on Windows (the service stops for the upgrade and starts again after): Windows does not let an update replace or move files a running program holds, so side-by-side updates are macOS and Linux only for now.

## 0.290.1

- **The Probe daemon is no longer refused its own start.** Since 0.285.2 the CLI's copy of the daemon-profile check could refuse `probe daemon worker`: the recorder starts the worker with the session's environment, and when that environment names the agent's session (a recorder started from the agent's own shell, or an agent that hands its hooks its session id) the check read the daemon as the agent and refused it, so no daemon ran in that session. The check now never refuses the daemon worker; an agent typing `probe daemon worker` is still refused by the plugin's hook.

## 0.290.0

- **A Claude Code session left open across a Probe plugin update uses the new plugin's skills, with no restart.** Claude Code reads Probe's skills from copies in its own skills folder (`~/.claude/skills`) and re-reads them when they change, but only a session start refreshed the copies, so a session open for days kept the old text (one loaded `plan-research-review` five hours after an update and missed its "log every run to Probe" rule). Now `probe update` and the Probe service's automatic update refresh the copies right after updating the plugin, so every open session's next skill call reads the new text. After an update made outside Probe (`/plugin update`, `claude plugin update`), the first call to a changed Probe skill refreshes the copies and is stopped once with a note asking the agent to call it again, which then loads the new text (that call would otherwise have used the text Claude Code already had); an agent is asked at most once per skill per session. The Skill call writes the copies only from the plugin Claude Code has installed, and leaves them alone while both Probe plugins are installed (a Who-records switch left half done); a session start on a copy Claude Code no longer has installed (an older version, or Codex's copy in a Codex session started from Claude Code) no longer puts its old text back. Codex needed no change: it lists a plugin's skills again on every turn from the version now installed. Sessions started before plugin 0.148.0 still need one restart. Probe also finds Claude Code's plugin list where `CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_CACHE_DIR` moves it (the hooks' hand-over, the skills refresh, the version checks).
- **Every Probe hook now reaches the Probe service, and a hook the service is not ready for costs less (tap 0.10.3).** When no warm hook process answers in time (the service is not running yet, or just restarted), the hook now runs only what your agent waits on (allow/block checks, context and messages) and hands the bookkeeping (usage telemetry, the status line's refresh, the team note's push) to the Probe service, which runs it once; with no service running it is saved in the service's queue and run when the service starts, and that same hook starts the service, so the next hook finds a warm process. Session end still runs in the hook itself, as before (Claude Code allows the whole step 1.5 s, Codex 3 s). A session set to `off` never starts the service. The transcript-capture plugin's prompt and turn-end hooks no longer start Python when nothing needs doing: about 5 ms instead of 25 ms per prompt, and 3.5 ms instead of 32 ms per turn end. New Probe service method `hooks.queue` (API v1, additive).

## 0.289.0

- **Tap 0.10.2.** Re-ships the 409 backoff (from the 0.288.0 entry about the recorder re-sending refused batches) to installs that updated to 0.10.1 in the 16 minutes before it merged (two changes both claimed 0.10.1).

- **`probe status`, `probe doctor`, turning capture off, `probe exec` and the version check now go through the Probe service.** `probe status` (in `--json`, a new `service` key) and `probe doctor` show what the service holds: whether it runs (version, pid), the sessions it has registered and their Probe mode, the sessions it records itself, its warm hook hosts, the runs in flight and its updater (a cycle running, the last check, why an update is deferred). With no service they say so and how it starts, and never start one; asking costs at most a second. Turning capture off for an agent now stops the recordings the service runs for that agent at once (it says how many) instead of at their next check. `probe exec` tells the service about the run it wraps, so the service's updater waits for it directly; the run lock stays for older services. A command that finds its cached release manifest stale asks the running service to refresh it instead of starting a background process of its own. With no service answering, an older one or Windows, each works as before.

## 0.288.0

- **Kimi Code's Probe hooks start faster, through the same dispatcher Claude Code and Codex use.** Kimi's plugin manifest had one hook per script (22 of them), each starting two fresh Python processes: a prompt started ten. It now has one hook per event, which puts Kimi's payload in Claude's shape once, runs that event's hooks through the dispatcher (in the warm process the Probe service keeps for the plugin folder, else in place, with the same budgets and merged output as Claude Code) and turns the result back into Kimi's format once. What Kimi sees is unchanged: the same refusals, the same context on a prompt, `/probe on` typed as a skill still flips the switch, and a daemon message is still never claimed after a tool call (Kimi drops that output) but delivered with the next prompt. Kimi has no hook approval step, so nothing needs re-approving; a Kimi session left open keeps its old per-script hooks, which still work, until it reloads plugins. The SessionStart hook now carries an explicit 60 s timeout (Kimi's default was 30 s), so the dispatcher always finishes inside it.
- **The recorder no longer re-sends a batch the server keeps refusing every tick (tap 0.10.1).** When the server answered 409 to a session's batch and checking its receipts could not settle it, every recorder on the machine sent the same batch again on its next tick, for good: one machine re-sent six refused sessions (one batch was 1.1 MB) about every 10 seconds, ~250 MB every half hour. Now that batch waits a minute before it goes again, then two, four and so on up to an hour, each wait shortened at random by up to a quarter so refused sessions do not re-send together.
